clue.text: Those in charge could be better — what hopes!

indicators.note: the letters could be something else entirely once rearranged, so this signals a shuffle of what follows

explanation.surface: A grumble that the people running things could do better, followed by a weary sigh of 'what hopes!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' is the anagram signal: BETTER WHAT HOPES rearranged gives the full phrase. The dash only separates the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for the authorities or people holding power, used for those running an organisation or country.

clue.text: Poor food in dining area — having no starter and lousy taste

parts.note: tack is old slang for food, especially poor fare (as in hardtack)
taken as written

indicators.note: the first letter of the dining-area word is dropped, its starter gone

parts.note: a mess is where service personnel eat

explanation.surface: A restaurant review: bad grub in the canteen, no starter offered, and generally dreadful taste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having no starter' trims MESS to ESS; 'starter' looks like a first course but means a first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tackiness is cheap, vulgar style, which is what lousy taste amounts to.

clue.text: Finishes posting — site initially down

indicators.note: the initial letter of 'site' moves down, to the bottom of this down entry

parts.note: posting a letter is sending it
its first letter is the one moved

explanation.surface: A note that a posting has ended, with the website itself initially down.
explanation.walkthrough: SENDING's opening S, the initial letter of 'site', drops to the foot of the down light, giving ENDINGS.
explanation.definitionFit: Finishes and endings are plural synonyms for the conclusions of things.

clue.text: No service in cathedral city? Plainly not!

parts.note: nought, zero, gives O
RN is the Royal Navy, one of the armed services
at means in, as in 'at home'
Ely is a Cambridgeshire cathedral city, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A complaint that no church service is held in a cathedral city, with a sardonic 'Plainly not!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'service' looks like worship but is the Royal Navy; 'in' gives AT, a standard equivalence.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornately means in a richly decorated way, the opposite of doing something plainly.

clue.text: Spaces start to appear in evacuation procedure

parts.note: an en is a printer's space half an em wide
an em is a printer's space the width of the letter M

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the following word is wanted

explanation.surface: Gaps begin to show during an emergency evacuation drill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spaces' gives two typographic spaces, EN and EM; 'evacuation' looks like leaving a building but means emptying the bowels.
explanation.definitionFit: An enema flushes out the bowels, a medical procedure for evacuating them.

clue.text: Fail to acknowledge good points of Flo?

definitions.text: Fail to acknowledge good points of Flo?

parts.words: Fail to acknowledge good points of Flo?
parts.note: Flo is a shortened Florence: to market her name in short form is a joke version of undervaluing someone

explanation.surface: Someone overlooks Flo's virtues.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as the idiom for undervaluing; the question mark flags the second reading, since Flo is literally a name sold in short form.
explanation.definitionFit: To undersell is to fail to acknowledge someone's merits; Flo is a shortened name, hence the pun.

clue.text: Name of that woman's husband

parts.note: her is the possessive for that woman
man is used for a husband, as in 'man and wife'

explanation.surface: Asking what that woman's husband is called.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Name' looks like an instruction to identify the husband; it is the definition, a man's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Herman is a male given name, so it is an example of a name.

clue.text: Most remarkable everyone's taking part in challenge?

indicators.note: the word for everyone joins in, sitting inside the challenge word

parts.note: a test is a challenge
all means everyone; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: Asking whether it is most impressive that everyone is joining in the challenge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most remarkable' works through 'tall story', an unlikely tale; the question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Tall means hard to believe, as in a tall tale, so the superlative is most remarkable.

clue.text: Order around — what my boss does about it

indicators.note: the boss's action goes around the abbreviation, holding it inside

parts.note: the setter's boss is the crossword editor, who edits
c, short for circa, means about

explanation.surface: The setter grumbles that the boss orders things around and keeps tinkering with it.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's boss is the editor, so the activity is EDIT; 'it' is the crossword being edited and joins the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An edict is an official decree, an order issued by authority.

clue.text: Dance round in church showing rhythm

indicators.note: the shuffled dance letters go in the middle of the church abbreviation

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: to dance round is to whirl about, so these letters are turned around into a new order

explanation.surface: A dance performed in the round inside a church shows off its rhythm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' looks like a circle of dancers but is the anagram signal; 'in' puts the shuffle inside the Church of England letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Cadence is the rise and fall or beat of speech or music, its rhythm.

clue.text: One previously learning the French for "siren"'

indicators.note: the other pieces come previously, before the numeral one, so it goes last

parts.note: lore is traditional knowledge or learning
le is French for the
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone who once studied French is looking for the word for siren.
explanation.walkthrough: 'previously' puts the other pieces before the numeral, so 'One' lands at the end despite leading the clue. The Lorelei is the Rhine maiden of German legend.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lorelei is a legendary Rhine maiden whose song lured boatmen to their deaths, a siren figure.

clue.text: Rugby players robbing banks — one's charged

indicators.note: the banks are the outer edges, robbed away from the team name

parts.note: the British and Irish Lions are a touring rugby union side

explanation.surface: Rugby players who rob banks, and one of them is charged by police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'robbing banks' strips the edges of LIONS; 'charged' sounds criminal but means electrically charged.
explanation.definitionFit: An ion is an atom or molecule carrying an electric charge, a particle with charge.

clue.text: Obvious replacement for Ant's partner

indicators.note: a replacement rearranges the letters, putting a new order in place of these words

explanation.surface: Finding a stand-in for Ant's partner (of the British TV duo Ant and Dec) is an easy call.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replacement for' rearranges ANTSPARTNER; the apostrophe is ignored. Ant and Dec are a British TV presenting duo.
explanation.definitionFit: Transparent means easily seen through, hence plain or evident.

clue.text: Country clubber on course to a meal ticket (love won't go the distance)

parts.note: Ernie Els is a South African golfer, who swings clubs on a course
LV is a luncheon voucher, a British meal ticket for workers

indicators.note: the word for love stops short, losing its final letter

parts.note: adore means love

explanation.surface: A golfer whose love of a free meal doesn't last the full round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clubber' suggests a nightclubber but is a golfer; 'won't go the distance' drops the end of ADORE to give ADOR.
explanation.definitionFit: El Salvador is a Central American nation, so it is an example of a country.

clue.text: AA named us in error, so it's very annoying

indicators.note: a mistake scrambles these letters into a wrong order

explanation.surface: The AA motoring organisation names us by mistake, which is infuriating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in error' rearranges AANAMEDUS; the AA is a British motoring breakdown service.
explanation.definitionFit: Ad nauseam means repeated to a tiresome, sickening extent, going on until it grates.

clue.text: Entering directions to store

indicators.note: the little word goes in, entering between the two compass letters

parts.note: S and W, south and west, are compass directions

explanation.surface: Instructions for getting into a shop, the directions to the store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'store' reads as a shop noun but is the verb, to put away.
explanation.definitionFit: To stow is to pack or put something away for keeping, a synonym of the verb to store.

clue.text: State is stopping John working? Wrong!

indicators.note: the little word plugs the gap, stopping up the toilet letters

parts.note: john is American slang for a toilet, which is a WC
on means operating or working
a sin is a wrong

explanation.surface: Someone protests that a state is stopping John from working, and that it is wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'John' looks like a man but is slang for the lavatory, WC.
explanation.definitionFit: Wisconsin is one of the fifty US states, in the Midwest.

clue.text: Acting poor — urge to adjourn for the time being

indicators.note: letters acting a part take on a new shape, so these are rearranged

explanation.surface: Some poor acting prompts an urge to call a halt for now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Acting' is the anagram signal on POOR URGE, the dash being punctuation only.
explanation.definitionFit: To prorogue a parliament is to suspend its sitting without dissolving it, a temporary halt.

clue.text: Here was dame with small chest

parts.note: S is the clothing abbreviation for small
an ark is a chest or coffer, as in the Ark of the Covenant

explanation.surface: Here lived a lady with a small bosom.
explanation.walkthrough: SARK is a Channel Island long ruled by a hereditary lord or dame, most famously Dame Sibyl Hathaway.
explanation.definitionFit: The Channel Island was governed by the Dame of Sark, so it is the place where a dame held sway.

clue.text: Bond reportedly stole gold

indicators.note: as people report it, by ear, the spoken phrase gives the entry

parts.note: a stole is a shawl or wrap; or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A news item: James Bond is said to have stolen gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stole' looks like a verb but is the scarf, a WRAP; WRAP OR said aloud is the French-derived word for a bond.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapport is a close, harmonious connection between people, a bond of understanding.

clue.text: Investments one relies on

parts.note: a unit is a single thing, one
trusts means relies on

explanation.surface: Investments that a person relies on.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a unit trust is a pooled investment fund, the US mutual fund equivalent.
explanation.definitionFit: These pooled funds sell units to savers, so they are a kind of investment vehicle.

clue.text: Attacks on supporters succeeded

indicators.note: in a down light one piece sits on top of another, so the abbreviation goes above

parts.note: s is the genealogical abbreviation for succeeded
allies are supporters

explanation.surface: Assaults on the backers worked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' places S above ALLIES in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sallies are sudden sorties or charges out against an enemy, so they are attacks.

clue.text: Pull woman Romeo's into

indicators.note: the letter goes into the word for woman, inside it

parts.note: wench is an old word for a young woman
Romeo is the NATO alphabet word for R; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: Pulling a woman Romeo fancies, a lothario's story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pull' looks like British slang for picking someone up but means a hard tug.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrench is a sudden violent twist or tug, a sharp pull.

clue.text: Rapper — he's up anyway for clerk

indicators.note: put any way at all, the letters may come in any order

explanation.surface: A rapper is up and about anyway, waiting for the clerk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' rearranges RAPPERHESUP; the apostrophe adds no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen-pusher or office clerk is a low-ranking worker shuffling documents, so the term fits a clerk.

clue.text: Given room but taken advantage of — that's not on

indicators.note: the little word on is not there, removed from the end

parts.note: put upon means exploited or taken advantage of

explanation.surface: A guest given a room but exploited protests that it's not acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's not on' looks like a British protest ('not acceptable') but literally removes ON.
explanation.definitionFit: To be put up is to be accommodated, given a bed or room for the night.

clue.text: Henry's a brave man taking over in chaos

parts.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

indicators.note: the brave man's letters take in the cricket letter, holding it inside

parts.note: a VC is a holder of the Victoria Cross, Britain's top medal for bravery
O is the cricket abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: Henry is a hero taking control amid the mayhem.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry is the SI unit H, not a king; VC is a medal holder, standing for Victoria Cross.
explanation.definitionFit: Havoc means widespread destruction and disorder, a synonym of chaos.

clue.text: Found in whole of house

indicators.note: the letters are found inside these clue words, spanning the gap between them

explanation.surface: Something discovered somewhere in the entire house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'house' looks like a building but is a house of the zodiac.
explanation.definitionFit: Leo is one of the twelve astrological signs, each called a house of the zodiac.

clue.text: Easily beat time on training run with Coe

indicators.note: training reshapes, so these letters are put through their paces into a new order

explanation.surface: Seb Coe, the British Olympic runner, sets a fast time on a training run and beats everyone easily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'training' rearranges RUN and COE to give ROUNCE; Coe is Sebastian Coe, the British Olympic middle-distance champion.
explanation.definitionFit: To trounce is to defeat heavily, winning with ease.

clue.text: Rivals eating chicken one day? Not these

definitions.text: Rivals eating chicken one day? Not these

indicators.note: the rivalry word eats, taking the other piece inside it

parts.note: vies means competes or rivals
an egg will be a chicken one day

explanation.surface: Competitors tucking into a chicken; vegetarians would never.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chicken one day' describes an egg, its future; the whole clue doubles as the definition, since vegetarians are those who won't eat the chicken.
explanation.definitionFit: Veggies, informal for vegetarians, do not eat meat such as chicken.

clue.text: Ruin the chances of those oafish Australians inspired by Don

indicators.note: breathed into the word for don, the pieces go inside it

parts.note: to don clothes is to put them on
them means those, colloquially
ockers are boorish, uncultivated Australians, in Australian slang

explanation.surface: Those loutish Aussies take their inspiration from Don Bradman, the great Australian batsman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' suggests Bradman but is the verb, to put on.
explanation.definitionFit: This idiom means to jinx or spoil a plan or someone's prospects.
